opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that the two workloads have very different shapes, even though on paper they both look like "running the model forward."

In pretraining, the system is designed around throughput on huge, regular batches. Everything is dense and predictable — fixed sequence lengths, fixed parallelism layout, and you're optimizing for keeping the compute saturated for weeks. The training framework assumes it owns the cluster and the memory layout.

RL rollout inference is almost the opposite. You're generating long, variable-length sequences, often agentic trajectories with tool calls and environment interaction, so the length distribution has a very long tail. A few rollouts can take ten times longer than the median, and that straggler problem dominates your efficiency. What you want there looks much more like a serving system — continuous batching, KV cache management, speculative decoding, maybe different parallelism and even lower precision than training uses.

So if you try to force one stack to do both, you end up compromising each. The training side wants stability and bit-level consistency; the inference side wants flexibility and latency tricks. And then there's the mismatch problem — if the inference engine's numerics drift from the training engine's, your policy is effectively off-policy, and you need corrections like importance sampling to keep RL stable.

In practice, I think the more realistic direction is not merging them into one engine, but making them decoupled and asynchronous — separate systems that are each very good at their job, with fast weight synchronization in between and careful handling of the numerical gap. That's harder engineering, but it scales better as rollouts get longer and more agentic.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts pretraining’s regular, throughput-focused batches with RL’s variable-length, tool-using rollouts and straggler challenges, attributing the separate systems to their different workload requirements.

r002.rationale: It says training prioritizes bit-level consistency while inference may use lower precision, and explains that numerical differences between engines can affect RL stability.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that they're optimizing for completely different things, and the hardware ends up telling you that.

In pretraining, inference barely exists as a separate concern. You're running forward passes on fixed sequences, you know the exact shape of every batch ahead of time, and the whole system is tuned for throughput over a static dataset. Nothing surprises you. The scheduler can pack sequences perfectly, the memory layout is predictable, and the only thing you care about is tokens per second per GPU over weeks.

RL inference is the opposite of that. The model is generating its own data, so sequence lengths are unknown until the rollout finishes. One sample stops after two hundred tokens, another goes on for eight thousand because it's reasoning through a hard math problem. You have this long-tail problem where the slowest rollout in the batch holds everyone else hostage. And on top of that you're constantly syncing weights from the training side, so your inference engine has to tolerate being interrupted and reloaded, which a pretraining pipeline never has to think about.

So when people ask why we don't just unify them, my view is that any unified system would be a compromise for both. The pretraining side wants determinism and dense utilization. The RL side wants elasticity, asynchronous scheduling, KV cache management for wildly varying lengths, and tight coupling with reward computation and the trainer. Those pull in opposite directions at the engineering level.

I'd also say the research questions are different. In RL, the inference engine is actually part of the algorithm. How you sample, how much off-policy drift you tolerate between the generating weights and the training weights, how you handle partial rollouts, all of that changes what the model learns. In pretraining, inference is just a tool for evaluation. It doesn't feed back into the gradient.

Could they converge eventually? Maybe, if the data mix shifts so heavily toward self-generated data that pretraining itself starts to look like RL. But right now I'd rather have two systems that are each very good at their job than one that's mediocre at both.

r001.rationale: The response explains that pretraining and RL need different system behavior and engineering capabilities, such as predictable throughput versus variable rollouts, asynchronous scheduling, and weight syncing.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute the separation to different precision requirements; it discusses throughput, scheduling, memory, and algorithmic differences instead.

astra-6.text:
I think they’ll remain separate because they’re optimizing for different things. In pretraining, the main workload is processing a large amount of fixed data efficiently. Inference during RL is part of a feedback loop: you generate responses, evaluate them, and use those results to update the model. So the model producing the data is constantly changing.

That creates different requirements. For RL, you care about rollout diversity, how long individual responses take, and how quickly you can get fresh results back into training. Maximizing inference throughput alone doesn’t necessarily make that loop more efficient—you can generate a lot of data that’s already stale by the time you use it.

They can share infrastructure and optimization techniques, but I don’t think that means they converge into one workload. The important distinction is whether you’re processing a fixed dataset or generating the next learning signal.

r001.rationale: The response describes different workload and feedback-loop requirements, such as rollout diversity and freshness, but does not attribute separation to different complexity requirements.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention precision requirements as a reason for keeping the workloads separate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they serve different objectives. In pretraining, inference is mostly about generating useful data at scale, so throughput and cost matter a lot. In RL, inference is part of a feedback loop: you generate trajectories, evaluate them, and update the policy. That makes policy freshness, exploration, and synchronization with training much more important.

They can share a lot of infrastructure, especially the underlying inference engine. But sharing an engine doesn’t necessarily mean they should become one system. The scheduling and data flow are different enough that I expect them to remain separate, while reusing more of the same components.

r001.rationale: The response describes different objectives, throughput needs, scheduling, and data flow, but does not attribute the separation to different complexity requirements.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention precision requirements as a reason for keeping the systems separate.
